The early life stages of Mediterranean parrotfish Sparisoma cretense begin with the release of small, pelagic eggs following broadcast spawning events. Upon hatching, the prolarvae emerge as yolk-sac larvae, relying entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the initial endotrophic phase. The wet weight at birth, which corresponds to the mass of the newly hatched yolk-sac larva, has been estimated at 0.00015 grams [Wwb = 0.00015 grams], a value derived from the egg diameter of a related scarine species. This minuscule starting mass places the species among the smaller-bodied teleost hatchlings within the family Labridae. The transition to exogenous feeding occurs shortly after mouth opening and swim bladder inflation, marking a critical period of high mortality. During these early pelagic stages, growth is rapid but highly dependent on local thermal conditions. Field studies conducted in the Mediterranean Sea documented that the gonadosomatic index (GSI) attains a value of approximately 4% [GSI = approximately 4%] when water temperatures average 17.1 °C [T = 17.1 °C].

As development proceeds through the larval and pre-metamorphic stages, Sparisoma cretense undergoes a series of morphological transformations culminating in a pelagic-benthic transition. Following settlement into suitable rocky or seagrass habitats, the post-settlement juveniles initiate a period of sustained somatic growth that continues until the attainment of sexual maturity. The total length at puberty, marking the onset of gonadal recrudescence and gametogenesis, has been recorded at 15.5 centimeters [Lp = 15.5 centimeters] in populations sampled around the Balearic Islands. This relatively modest size at maturity reflects the species' intermediate position within the size spectrum of Mediterranean labrids, neither as diminutive as the small-bodied wrasses nor as large as the more robust members of the family. Correspondingly, the wet weight at puberty was estimated at 48.5 grams [Wwp = 48.5 grams] using a length-weight relationship derived from local specimens. This value provides a useful benchmark for comparing the energetic demands of reproductive maturation across different populations. The consistency of these estimates across multiple sampling years suggests a relatively stable life-history strategy for this species under current thermal regimes.

The adult phase of the life cycle is characterized by a prolonged period of iteroparous reproduction and continued, albeit decelerated, somatic growth. The ultimate total length, representing the asymptotic size approached by older individuals, has been measured at 50 centimeters [Li = 50 centimeters] in extensive surveys of fully grown adults. This maximum recorded length establishes Sparisoma cretense as one of the larger parrotfish species inhabiting the Mediterranean basin, with only a few congeners attaining comparable dimensions. The corresponding ultimate wet weight, derived from the length-weight allometry, reaches approximately 1800 grams [Wwi = approximately 1800 grams] in the largest documented individuals. This substantial body mass supports a significant gonadal output during each spawning season and underscores the species' role as a keystone herbivore in coastal ecosystems. The growth trajectory from the 0.00015 gram hatchling to the 1800 gram adult represents a remarkable increase of over seven orders of magnitude, a testament to the efficiency of planktivory and subsequent browsing on algal turfs that fuels this dramatic expansion in biomass throughout the life span.

Reproductive effort is partitioned across multiple spawning events each year, with spawning activity peaking during the warmer months. The maximum lifespan of Sparisoma cretense has been estimated from otolith increment analysis and mark-recapture studies. In the thermally stable conditions of the eastern Mediterranean, where annual water temperatures average 17.1 °C [T = 17.1 °C], the species has been documented to achieve a lifespan of approximately 7300 days [am = approximately 7300 days], which corresponds to roughly twenty years. This longevity is noteworthy among Mediterranean reef fishes and positions the species as a relatively slow-living member of the parrotfish guild. The extended adult phase allows for multiple reproductive seasons, which likely buffers population dynamics against sporadic recruitment failures. Annual reproductive output is consequently structured over a considerable number of breeding cycles, with each gravid female contributing to the next generation over many consecutive years. The repeated spawning events during the adult phase represent a significant energetic investment, and the species' ability to sustain this effort over two decades highlights the efficiency of its foraging ecology and the productivity of its algal grazing grounds.

Comparisons with other labrid species reveal that the life-history strategy of Sparisoma cretense is shaped by the relatively stable thermal environment it inhabits. The gonadosomatic index was approximately 4% [GSI = approximately 4%] under those same thermal conditions of 17.1 °C [T = 17.1 °C]. Individuals typically reach sexual maturity at a body length of 15.5 cm [Lp = 15.5 cm] and a corresponding wet weight at puberty of 48.5 grams [Wwp = 48.5 grams], representing the size thresholds at which individuals shift from purely somatic growth to a mixed strategy of growth and reproduction. These benchmarks are essential for demographic modeling and for assessing the impact of size-selective fishing pressure on spawning stock biomass. The asymptotic length of 50 cm [Li = 50 cm] and the adult body mass ceiling of 1800 grams [Wwi = 1800 grams] define the upper limits of the species' size range and serve as reference points for comparing body condition across populations. The combination of a small birth mass, moderate size at maturity, large adult size, and exceptional longevity of 7300 days [am = 7300 days] portrays Sparisoma cretense as a classic example of a temperate-zone teleost with a conservative, long-generation life history at a temperature of 17.1 °C [T = 17.1 °C].
